awd_titl_txt: IRES Track I: US-Canada Collaborative Research on Biomaterials for stem cell culture and neural differentiation
awd_abstract_narration:
This award supports international research experiences for U.S. undergraduate students from the University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP) at the University of Victoria (UVic) in Canada in interdisciplinary research representing the fields of bioengineering and neuroscience. The project engages primarily Hispanic engineering students at UTEP, a majority Hispanic 4-year, public institution. Reciprocal visits to UTEP by UVic students will be supported with Canadian funds.  UTEP students will be afforded professional development and educational opportunities in cutting-edge research.  Specifically, the project engages the synergism of stem cell biology with advanced 3-dimensional biomaterial technology to manufacture tissue from stem cells. Generating patient-specific "artificial" tissue allows the researchers to control the rate of growth and differentiation of stem cells.  This research is significant in paving the way for modeling disease and for future drug development.  

Working together, the interdisciplinary team aims to identify unique approaches of targeting differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells [iPSCs] into neural phenotypes by utilizing advanced materials and processing. Specifically, the UTEP team has expertise in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) culture and 3D bioprinting, and UVic has expertise in culturing neuronal differentiation of human iPSC on fibrin-based scaffolds. The research focus is the application of microfluidic-based 3D bioprinting for coprinting of human iPSCs together with biomaterial scaffolds to generate bio-composites of the desired architecture with high fidelity. Bioprinting iPSCs with advanced biomaterials and scaffolds bears the promise to develop 3D tissues, ideally including encapsulated cells and facilitating their proliferation, and targeted differentiation. The project enables addressing critical questions in the field: 1) How can advanced materials and their unique designs facilitate stem cell culture and promote their differentiation? 2) How can 3D bioprinting be applied as an advanced manufacturing technique to mimic the complex environment for regulating growth and differentiation of stem cells? 3) Does the differentiated progeny of cells cultured atop micro-textured scaffolds exhibit enhanced functionality and phenotype, compared with controls? Thus, the scientific goal is to better understand the role of growth factors and micro-environmental niche and cues released from biomaterial scaffolds in the regulation of adult human iPSC differentiation into neural phenotypes. It is widely known that distractive biomaterial scaffolds that incorporate patterned structures and specific compartments of growth factors can more intricately guide stem cell development. Achieving this goal enables the ability to address fundamental neurobiological questions about neuronal growth, differentiation, which is essential for designing treatments for nervous system disorders or traumatic brain injury.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Intellectual Merit

The IRES: UTEP-UVIC program significantly advanced our scientific understanding by focusing on the co-printing of human stem cell-derived products with biomedical scaffolds using 3D bioprinting technology, thereby contributing to the development of innovative methodologies in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. The initiative fostered international collaboration between the University of Texas at El Paso and the University of Victoria, enhancing cross-border scientific exchange and enriching the research experience for undergraduate students. Through hands-on laboratory training and mentor-guided research, students gained critical skills in cell culture, bioprinting, and experimental design. The program culminated in seven peer-reviewed publications and six conference presentations, demonstrating the scholarly impact and rigor of the research conducted.

Broader Impacts

The program made substantial contributions to broadening participation in STEM by engaging undergraduate students from the US Southwest Border region, with a focus on marginalized and underrepresented populations. By providing international research experiences and structured mentorship, the initiative supported students’ academic progression and professional development, preparing them for graduate education and careers in STEM fields. The integration of graduate-undergraduate working groups fostered collaborative learning and peer mentorship, while the international component cultivated global competencies essential for today’s STEM workforce. Despite challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, the program adapted effectively, maintaining its commitment to student success and research productivity. Overall, the program demonstrated that early, immersive research experiences are pivotal for holistic student development, fostering scientific curiosity, resilience, and long-term engagement in research and innovation.

Outcomes

The IRES: UTEP-UVIC program, funded by the National Science Foundation in 2018, successfully achieved its goal of providing international research experiences to undergraduate STEM students, particularly those from the US Southwest Border region and underrepresented communities. Over the three-year grant period, the program:

  • Trained 15 undergraduate students through immersive, hands-on research experiences in both the United States and Canada.
  • Advanced scientific research in 3D bioprinting by co-printing human stem cell-derived products with biomedical scaffolds, contributing to the field of tissue engineering.
  • Established graduate-undergraduate working groups, fostering mentorship, collaboration, and peer learning.
  • Prepared students for post-baccalaureate education, with many participants pursuing graduate studies or entering STEM careers.
  • Strengthened international research collaborations between UTEP and UVIC, promoting cross-cultural scientific exchange.
  • Produced seven peer-reviewed publications and six conference presentations, showcasing the quality and impact of student-led research.
  • Adapted to challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, maintaining program continuity and student engagement through flexible and resilient strategies.
  • Demonstrated significant academic and professional growth among participants, affirming the value of early research experiences in shaping career trajectories and fostering lifelong engagement with science.

Overall, the program contributed meaningfully to the development of a diverse, globally engaged STEM workforce and highlighted the transformative potential of undergraduate research in promoting access and equity, excellence and innovation.
